subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Neglect of Probability
description: A fast breakdown of Neglect of Probability for builders.

hook.text: After 9/11, Americans drove instead of flew. Car crash deaths spiked by 1,600 the next year.

buildup.text: Flying remained far safer, but the vivid terror of a plane attack overwhelmed cold statistics.

discovery.text: Probability neglect: we react to how bad an outcome sounds, ignoring how unlikely it is.

twist.text: A shark attack kills 5 people a year. Vending machines kill 13. We fear sharks and hug vending machines.

climax.text: Drama captures attention. Probability doesn't. Our fear is calibrated to vividness, not to data.

punchline.text: Scary isn't the same as likely.

quiz.question: What does neglect of probability cause?
options: We overreact to vivid but rare events

details.summary: Neglect of probability is the tendency to ignore actual likelihood and make decisions based on the possibility or vividness of an outcome rather than its statistical probability. People treat a one percent risk and a fifty percent risk similarly if the outcome is emotionally vivid.
details.whyItMatters: When people ignore probabilities, they overreact to rare dramatic risks like terrorism while underreacting to common mundane risks like heart disease. This distortion misallocates personal and government resources toward the wrong threats.
takeaways: Vivid outcomes receive attention regardless of their actual probability
People treat low-probability events as either impossible or certain
Emotional reactions overwhelm rational probability assessment

faq.question: Why do people fear plane crashes more than car accidents?
faq.answer: Plane crashes are vivid, dramatic, and heavily reported despite being extremely rare. Car accidents are mundane and common. The emotional intensity of imagining a plane crash overwhelms the statistical reality that driving is far more dangerous.

faq.question: How does probability neglect affect policy?
faq.answer: Governments spend disproportionately on dramatic low-probability risks like terrorism while underfunding responses to common killers like pollution and road safety. Public demand driven by fear rather than data distorts resource allocation.
